Quick Read

RIVN beat earnings expectations with revenue up 38% to $2.16B, but still lost $913M and its stock remains down 42% this year.

Rivian refused to break out R2 delivery numbers separately, raising transparency concerns while its pricier R1T and R1S models are presumed to be selling poorly.

The US EV market shrank 30% in the first three quarters of the year, with EVs representing only 6% of new car sales, while TSLA holds over 50% market share.

Read More: Avoid these 13 retirement mistakes before they derail your future (sponsor)

Rivian (NASDAQ: RIVN) posted better-than-expected earnings. Its R2 SUV has shown sales promise. Neither masks the fact that the EV company's stock is down 42% this year, although it will get a small piece of that share back because of its modest quarterly success. And, despite an improvement at the bottom line, Rivian lost $913 million.

Rivian was proud of its revenue performance. It rose 38% to $2.16 billion. And, indeed, the bottom line improved. It lost $1.17 billion in the same period last year.

Spencer Platt / Getty Images

What may concern investors most is that Rivian did not change its top-line delivery guidance. Before earnings, the range was 65,000 to 70,000. In the earnings announcement, it raised the range to 67,000 to 70,000. And, despite comments about R2 sales, the disclosure was less specific. "We had record deliveries, with R2 delivering much of the gain quarter-over-quarter." Rivian did not break out the R2 numbers from total deliveries, and it could have.

Presumably, its sales of the expensive R1T and R1S continue to be poor.

Rivian remains one of the two US EV companies with a grim future. The other is Lucid (NASDAQ: LCID).

Rivian's unit deliveries would need to go well into the hundreds of thousands for it to make money, and it is swimming against a strong tide.

The era of humanoid robots isn't on the distant horizon any longer. It's almost upon us, and in some regards already here. Demonstrations of them are now common, and Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) co-founder and CEO Elon Musk still believes his company will be making 20,000 Optimus robots per week by the end of next year.

The opportunity is getting investment capital flowing, of course. The next chapter in this business's overall funding? The debut of Agility Robotics' stock sometime in November.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Just don't dive in as soon as you can. You'll likely be able to get it at a lower price soon enough.

The SPAC route

This won't be your typical IPO (initial public offering). Rather, privately owned Agility Robotics will go public by being absorbed into a special purpose acquisition company -- or "SPAC" -- called Churchill Capital XI (NASDAQ: CCXI), specifically created for this purpose and that's already trading. Once that $620 million SPAC offering is completed (valuing Agility at $2.5 billion), its name and ticker will be changed to Agility Robotics and AGLT, respectively.

Image source: Agility Robotics.

This is an easier way to become a publicly traded entity than a conventional IPO, in which a company must meet strict listing requirements before selling newly issued shares to investors.

Again, though, don't feel as if you need to be first in line to invest.

Let someone else insist on being first at any price

Although the process is somewhat different, the underlying hype that usually surrounds new high-profile stocks is the same. That is, as we recently saw with Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX) and Lycia Therapeutics (NASDAQ: LYCA), it doesn't take long for the initial bullishness stemming from newness to fade, allowing young stocks to lose quite a bit of ground early on. Agility Robotics' SPAC isn't apt to be an exception.

Just don't feel as if you need to avoid Agility Robotics forever. Although post-listing volatility could linger for years, the most harrowing action is often in the rearview mirror within a few weeks, if not several days. Steering clear of this initial action is purely a practical matter meant to avoid fairly predictable profit-taking.

title: Tesla’s Cybercab Costs “About $25,000” to Build. Waymo Has a Big Problem: It’s Cost Is Nearly 4X That
detail:
Tesla’s Cybercab Costs “About $25,000” to Build. Waymo Has a Big Problem: It’s Cost Is Nearly 4X That
Gian Estrada

TSLA
GOOG
UBER
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Tesla's Cybercab Costs "About $25,000" to Build. Waymo Has a Big Problem: It's Cost Is Nearly 4X That ©U.S. Air Force photo and Bl∡ke from Pexels via Canva]
Key Takeaways

Tesla's Cybercab costs about $25,000 to produce, against upward of $100,000 for each of Alphabet's Waymo vehicles, according to Prof G Markets' Dan Chiolan.

That gap lets Tesla put about four robotaxis on the road for the price of one of Waymo's current cars, an edge that shrinks against Waymo's cheaper new Ojai but doesn't disappear.

Waymo still drives about seven times Tesla's weekly miles, though investor Jason Calacanis expects Tesla to take more of the market than Waymo or Uber.

Tesla trades at 190x forward earnings, well above its three-year average of 136x, so the stock already prices in a lot of robotaxi success.

Elon Musk doesn't think Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ) has been in a robotaxi race at all.

When Jason Scharf posted on X that "the battle for Autonomous Austin might already be over," Musk replied: "It was never a real contest."

That's a bold thing to say about Alphabet (GOOG), whose Waymo gives more than 500,000 paid rides a week and is still well ahead by almost any measure. But on the Oct. 28 episode of Prof G Markets, Dan Chiolan pointed to the one edge that could make Musk right:

"those Tesla Cybercabs cost about $25,000 to produce, whereas Waymo's cost upward of $100,000."

So Tesla can put about four robotaxis on the road for the price of one of Waymo's current cars.

(October was a good month for the stock, too: Tesla rose 13% in October, the best in the Magnificent Seven, on SpaceX merger talk and a Barclays upgrade that also pointed to growing Robotaxi activity. It's still down for the year, though, the worst in the group.)

Waymo Still Has the Miles

Chiolan was clear that Tesla is behind. "Waymo does about seven times the amount of miles that Tesla does weekly," he said. Waymo now runs paid rides in 15 U.S. cities, he noted.

Tesla now runs its Robotaxi without safety monitors in six cities. On Sept. 3, it started putting Cybercabs on the road in Austin: its purpose-built robotaxi, with no steering wheel or pedals. And its cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles reached nearly 2 million by the end of the third quarter.

That design has drawn federal scrutiny. NHTSA opened an investigation in early September into how Tesla certified the Cybercab without those controls, and Tesla's sworn answers were due Oct. 30. A bad outcome could slow the rollout the cost math depends on.

So "never a real contest" is a stretch, at least on miles. But Waymo built that lead with expensive cars. Chiolan puts the price gap down to Waymo's much heavier load of sensors, which also makes its cars harder and slower to build. Waymo is working on that: its new Ojai van uses 42% fewer sensors than the Jaguar it replaces, and Waymo has said the new hardware costs under $20,000 per car. Outside estimates for the whole Ojai run from about $50,000 to $125,000, and Waymo hasn't confirmed a total. Against that range, Tesla still gets two to five Cybercabs for every Ojai.

Tesla Investment Narrative Recap

To own Tesla today, you need to believe the heavy spending on autonomy, chips and energy eventually turns into higher margin software and services on top of the EV base. The short term swing factor is clear. Investors are watching whether Cybercab and FSD usage build quickly enough to justify elevated R&D and capex while auto margins stay under pressure.

Recent Q3 numbers showed revenue broadly flat year on year and net income and EPS lower, while capital intensity and free cash flow strain remain key watchpoints. In that context, the biggest risk is that tariffs, softer deliveries or slower autonomy monetisation keep margins subdued, turning this investment phase into a prolonged drag rather than a bridge to better profitability.

The Turo partnership for verified FSD Supervised rentals plugs directly into that autonomy thesis. If renters convert into long term FSD subscribers on their own vehicles, it could support the push toward recurring software revenue that sits behind the Cybercab and robotaxi story. It also gives Tesla more real world data and a higher profile for FSD at a time when R&D spending, margin pressure and regulatory scrutiny on autonomy all remain central to the execution risk.

What The Tesla Cybercab Story Is Asking You To Underwrite

Tesla's narrative now leans heavily on analysts' expectation that the business can scale from an EV manufacturer with pressured auto margins into a platform that supports large software and services streams such as FSD, Cybercab and energy. detail:
Tesla's Cybercab Reaches Dallas in November, and Nevada Just Cleared 5,000 Robotaxis in Las Vegas. Here's the Number That Makes the Bulls Right.
Jeff Siegel, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 8:05 PM CDT 3 min read

Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) plans to expand its Cybercab presence in Dallas in November, beyond its initial expanded deployment in Austin. Meanwhile, Nevada regulators have authorized Tesla to operate up to 5,000 fully autonomous vehicles in the Las Vegas area during its first year under the new permit.

But the bigger question isn't how many robotaxis Tesla can put on the road. It's how much money each vehicle can generate.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The magic number is $0.30

During Tesla's Q3 earnings call, CFO Vaibhav Taneja reiterated the company's goal of reducing robotaxi operating costs to approximately $0.30 per paid mile. Tesla hasn't reached that target yet. But consider the potential economics if it does.

Image source: Getty Images.

During Tesla's 2024 Cybercab unveiling, Elon Musk projected passenger fares of approximately $0.30 to $0.40 per mile. At $0.40 per mile, a robotaxi completing 50,000 paid miles annually would generate $20,000 in revenue. Assuming Tesla achieves its $0.30-per-mile operating cost target, each Cybercab could generate $5,000 in profits (before any additional expenses).

Now consider Tesla's longer-term ambitions. Musk's compensation plan includes a milestone requiring an average of at least 1 million robotaxis in commercial operation over three consecutive months. At that scale, assuming each vehicle completes 50,000 paid miles annually at a fare of $0.40 per mile, Tesla could theoretically generate $20 billion in annual gross passenger fares. Achieving its $0.30-per-paid-mile operating cost target would leave approximately $5 billion in annual contribution before taxes and any additional expenses.

Tesla still has plenty to prove

Those figures are just rough estimates and assume significant vehicle utilization. Tesla also has to demonstrate that its Cybercabs can operate safely, reliably, and profitably at scale.

Management expects robotaxis to begin making a noticeable financial contribution in Q2 2027. So if you're bullish on Tesla, the $0.30-per-mile target is the number to watch. If Tesla can hit that target while maintaining strong utilization and pricing, robotaxis could eventually become a substantial source of recurring profits.

title: Could Rivian's Model 3 Moment Be Coming? Tesla Stock Climbed 1,364% in 3 Years.
detail:
Could Rivian's Model 3 Moment Be Coming? Tesla Stock Climbed 1,364% in 3 Years.
Daniel Miller, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 12:03 PM CDT 5 min read
RIVN
TSLA
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Rivian Automotive (NASDAQ: RIVN) investors have plenty riding on the recently launched and highly anticipated R2, and selling more vehicles would certainly be welcome. But the bigger prize is what could happen when the company gets more efficient at building them.

Fortunately, we have precedent from a fellow electric vehicle (EV) maker. Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) offers a compelling example. Its Model 3 production breakthrough helped set the stage for a much more profitable business -- and shareholders enjoyed a roller-coaster stock price ride along the way.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Could Rivian be approaching a similar turning point? There are encouraging signs, but the answer depends on more than customers wanting an R2. Let's dig in.

Rewind to Tesla's breakthrough

During the second quarter of 2018, Tesla's Model 3 gross margin turned slightly positive. Management credited lower labor hours, reduced ramp-up costs, better absorption of fixed costs, and lower material costs. Only one quarter later, Model 3 gross margin exceeded 20%, while labor hours per vehicle fell more than 30% sequentially. That happened even as Tesla shifted production toward more complex all-wheel-drive versions.

Tesla wasn't simply building more cars. It was using fewer labor hours to build each one. That doesn't necessarily mean its total labor hours declined, but it shows how a smoother production process can improve vehicle economics, requiring less labor time per vehicle.

Tesla's financial transformation quickly followed. Between the third quarter of 2018 and the third quarter of 2021, Tesla's company-wide operating margin increased from 6.1% to 14.6%. Between Sept. 28, 2018, and Sept. 30, 2021 -- the corresponding quarter-end trading dates -- its split-adjusted stock price climbed approximately 1,364%.

TSLA data by YCharts

Rivian shareholders would certainly take a helping of that, maybe even seconds. More importantly, Tesla's return reflected much more than one successful production ramp-up, and it certainly is not a forecast or prediction for Rivian. The useful lesson is how much the investment story can change when a promising vehicle becomes a profitable business.

Does Rivian have the demand?

Rivian will need ample demand to create its own Model 3 moment with its very own R2, and the early signals for R2 demand are encouraging. During its second-quarter earnings call, Rivian said reservation-to-order conversion for the roughly $58,000 R2 Launch Edition was meaningfully higher than management expected. It didn't disclose the conversion percentage, but that's a positive sign for the initial version before more affordable models of the R2 enter production.

Space Exploration Technologies and Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) CEO Elon Musk has given shares of Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) a terrific boost after his latest post on X, formerly Twitter.

While replying to a post by an analyst at Citrini Research, which provides thematic equity investing and macro trading insights, Musk pointed out that the dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) needed in humanoid robots "will exceed everything else on Earth." Micron stock surged more than 5% following Musk's remark.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

In this article, we will check if humanoids can indeed become the next major growth driver for the memory industry and Micron Technology.

Image source: Getty Images.

Robots can become the next big catalyst for the memory industry

According to Counterpoint Research, DRAM demand from humanoids could increase by almost 21x between 2026 and 2030. The research firm notes that the DRAM content in each humanoid could jump from the current 19GB to 39GB by the end of the decade.

However, Musk believes that humanoids will need much larger DRAM. Tesla, for instance, uses 72GB of memory on its AI5 chip that powers the Optimus robot, while the AI6 chip is equipped with 144GB of memory. It is worth noting that Musk had to slash the AI5's memory capacity in half, while the AI6 chip saw a one-third drop in memory capacity. Tesla had to make this move to procure enough memory volumes and reduce production costs amid the ongoing memory shortage.

What's worth noting is that Tesla has begun production of Optimus and intends to start shipping to customers next year. Musk predicts that Tesla can produce a million units of its humanoids every year at the Fremont factory. Moreover, demand for autonomous robots is increasing in factories.

Toyota, for instance, aims to automate its factories by deploying 400,000 robots. Meanwhile, Goldman Sachs recently increased its humanoid sales forecast for 2035 by a whopping 5x. The investment bank estimates that shipments of humanoid robots could reach 6.5 million units in 2035, generating $138 billion in revenue.

As such, there is a strong likelihood that humanoids will sustain robust demand for memory chips over the long run, adding to existing catalysts such as data centers, smartphones, vehicles, and personal computers.

title: SpaceX Is Considering a Merger With Tesla. Here's Why That Would Be a Bad Move.
detail:
SpaceX Is Considering a Merger With Tesla. Here's Why That Would Be a Bad Move.
Brett Schafer, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 4:20 AM CDT 5 min read
SPCX
TSLA
NVDA

Trading disclosure

The final move may be about to unfold. Elon Musk has set plans in motion to potentially merge his two industrial giants: Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX) and Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA). A merger has not been formally announced, but each company has formed an independent committee to explore the potential benefits of a merger. It is more likely than not to go through within the next year.

Two trillion-dollar market cap stocks merging would consummate the largest corporate marriage in history. I think it would be a terrible idea. Here's why.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Minimal business overlap

Regardless of what the merger presentation says, there is little overlap between Tesla's and SpaceX's businesses today.

SpaceX has its launch business, connectivity (Starlink), and is investing in artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. It is investing in AI software services like Grok Bot in hopes of carving out a place in the AI race. Tesla sells electric vehicles and battery packs and is working on autonomous driving and humanoid robot technologies.

One might argue that the future Optimus humanoid robot could utilize Starlink to connect to the internet, or that Tesla battery packs could be used at SpaceX AI data centers. However, just because one business can sell a product to another does not mean the two should merge simply because they share the same chief executive officer.

Adding so many product lines under one corporate umbrella is not going to make the two businesses more valuable; it will muddy the waters and confuse any investor trying to decide whether to buy the stock.

Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Image source: Getty Images.
Raiding Tesla's balance sheet for capital spending

SpaceX's revenue is soaring, posting 161% growth last quarter. Tesla, not so much. Its revenue was little changed year over year, with declining operating earnings, and its revenue has been stagnant for many years. Its earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) peaked in 2022 and have declined ever since.

So why does Musk want to merge it with SpaceX? It is likely due to the $45 billion in cash on Tesla's balance sheet. SpaceX is in the midst of a huge spending spree on data centers, which is a large cash drain for the business. This is why it did the biggest initial public offering (IPO) earlier this year, raised more debt in recent weeks, and might acquire Tesla.

A SpaceX and Tesla Merger Will Only Be Successful If This One Thing Happens

Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX) and Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) are both exploring a merger between the two companies. While both have been run separately by Elon Musk for years, the eccentric technology founder now believes it may be ideal to have the two businesses under one corporate umbrella. Each business has a separate committee exploring the prospects of a deal.

Increasingly, the companies are collaborating on projects, including the recently announced Terrafab semiconductor production venture. If a merger between the two companies is to be consummated, semiconductor manufacturing is key to lasting success. Here's why.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Scaling chip production

Terrafab is just an idea today, a joint venture formed between SpaceX, Tesla, and Intel, with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing rumored to be in talks to join the project. Musk and the team have plans to build a massive manufacturing base in Texas for computer chips.

These chips will power the future of Tesla and SpaceX products and are a reason for the merger. These could include Tesla electric vehicles, the Optimus humanoid robot, Starlink satellites, and the data centers SpaceX is beginning to build for artificial intelligence (AI).

However, this is a long-term project, with production not planned until 2028 at the earliest. When this happens, SpaceX hopes to have engineered the ability to produce space-based data centers at a lower cost-to-serve than terrestrial competitors. If it can do so while powering these data centers with its own computer chips, this vertical integration could be a valuable competitive advantage for the combined SpaceX-Tesla business.

Image source: Getty Images.
Tesla's financial state

The question remains: Why is Tesla needed for this space-based data center project, which is powered by internal computer chips? Sure, Tesla could use Terrafab's computer chips for its vehicles or to train its AI models for self-driving cars, but this isn't something it needs to do internally for the business to function, and it has nothing to do with SpaceX's ambitions.

What Musk and SpaceX likely want from Terrafab and the forthcoming Tesla and SpaceX merger is the cash on Tesla's balance sheet, which numbered $45 billion at the end of last quarter. However, the Tesla business itself is struggling, with operating income falling 56% last quarter. Revenue is not growing either, with promises of self-driving technology and the Optimus humanoid robot not appearing on today's financial statements.

It is not necessarily what SpaceX can do for Tesla, but what Tesla can provide to SpaceX in the form of capital, that is the reason for this merger exploration.

Should the two companies even merge?

If a Tesla-SpaceX merger occurs, much will rest on this Terrafab joint venture to ensure its success. It is part of a grand plan by Musk and SpaceX to build a massive orbital satellite and AI data center network. However, there are a ton of steps that need to occur before this happens, such as proving that Terrafab can actually manufacture working chips or getting orbital data centers functional.

Adding Tesla to the picture under one corporate umbrella might just make the story messier than it needs to be. There are many uncertainties in the story involving both companies. Sure, SpaceX could use Tesla's cash balance to fund its growth ambitions, but that should not be the only reason for a merger. Terrafab is an interesting idea, but all it is today -- along with many other business lines at Tesla and SpaceX -- is an idea, one that faces huge upfront capital commitments and technical challenges.

Plus, from an investor perspective, both stocks trade at premium valuations. Tesla's price-to-earnings ratio (P/E) is in the hundreds, and SpaceX trades at a $2 trillion market cap compared to trailing revenue of $33 billion. A merger may make sense if you believe in the Terrafab project, but there are so many uncertainties across the board with these two businesses that I think both stocks are ones to avoid right now.
